unit.why: A short anecdote, quoted from the preface to Semikhat Moshe, about the Hakham Tzvi, a non-Hasidic rabbinic authority: he always read the honorific titles on letters sent to him so that shame would keep him from sinning.

stories.end_quote: ויהי׳ לו בושה לעשות עבירה עכ״ל
stories.summary_en: The Hakham Tzvi always read the praising titles written on letters addressed to him, and when a close associate asked why, he explained that seeing himself lauded as a great sage would make him ashamed to commit a sin.

tags.why: Laudatory anecdote about the Hakham Tzvi, a non-Hasidic rabbinic authority, quoted from an earlier book.
Shame is used deliberately as a safeguard against sin.
The anecdote illustrates a pious technique for guarding against sin.
It sits in an ethical-instruction context (the next division is on anger), but it has no explicit 'from this we learn' frame.
Its subject is a non-Hasidic rabbinic figure, although no Hasidic interaction is shown.
